objectives: By the end of the week, students will explain how triangle area relates to parallelogram area, identify a base and its corresponding perpendicular height, use A = (b × h) ÷ 2 to find triangle areas, and find polygon areas by decomposing them into simpler shapes. Students will explain their reasoning and label areas in square units.
agenda:
Day 1 – Monday: Lesson 7 – From Parallelograms to Triangles
Split a parallelogram along a diagonal into two congruent triangles. Use diagrams to explain why each triangle has half the area of the parallelogram.

Day 2 – Tuesday: Lesson 8 – Area of Triangles
Find triangle areas by composing two congruent copies into a parallelogram or by decomposing shapes with known areas. Compare strategies with a partner and explain your reasoning.

Day 3 – Wednesday: Lesson 9 – Formula for the Area of a Triangle
Explain the one-half factor in A = (b × h) ÷ 2. Use the formula to calculate triangle areas and label answers in square units.

Day 4 – Thursday: Lesson 10 – Bases and Heights of Triangles
Choose a base and identify or draw its corresponding perpendicular height. Find heights inside or outside a triangle, extending the base when needed, and distinguish height from a slanted side length.

Day 5 – Friday: Lesson 11 – Polygons
Find polygon areas by decomposing figures into non-overlapping triangles, rectangles, or parallelograms and adding their areas. Compare different decompositions and justify why they give the same total area.
homework: Complete assigned DeltaMath practice. Review your notes on triangle area, bases and heights, and polygon decomposition. Bring your notebook, paper, and a sharpened pencil to class every day.
languageObjectives: Students will explain the relationship between triangle and parallelogram areas using the terms congruent, one-half, base, and height.
Students will describe how a height is perpendicular to its corresponding base or the line containing that base.
Students will compare and justify polygon area strategies using the terms decompose, non-overlapping, polygon, and square units.

objectives: By the end of the week, students will calculate the area of parallelograms, use the properties of parallelograms to find missing side and angle measures, and classify different types of quadrilaterals.
agenda:
Day 1 – Monday: Area of Parallelograms
Identify a base and its corresponding perpendicular height, then use A = b × h to find the area of a parallelogram. Explain how cutting and rearranging a parallelogram forms a rectangle with the same area.

Day 2 – Tuesday: Parallelogram Properties and Quadrilaterals
Use the facts that opposite sides are parallel and congruent, opposite angles are congruent, and consecutive angles are supplementary to find missing side and angle measures. Classify and label parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses, squares, trapezoids, and other quadrilaterals.

Day 3 – Wednesday: Applying Parallelogram Relationships
Solve problems involving area, missing bases or heights, missing side lengths, and missing angle measures. Justify each answer using a parallelogram property.

Day 4 – Thursday: Quiz Review
Complete mixed practice on parallelogram area, angle relationships, side relationships, and quadrilateral classification. Ask questions and correct misunderstandings before the quiz.

Day 5 – Friday: Quiz
Demonstrate your understanding of parallelogram area and properties and the classification of quadrilaterals.
homework: Complete assigned DeltaMath or review practice. Bring your notebook, paper, and a sharpened pencil to class every day. Study Thursday's review for Friday's quiz.
languageObjectives: Students will explain how a base and its corresponding perpendicular height determine the area of a parallelogram.
Students will justify missing measures and classifications using the terms opposite, consecutive, parallel, congruent, supplementary, and quadrilateral.

objectives: By the end of the week, students will explain the meaning of area and use tiling, decomposing, rearranging, enclosing, and subtracting to find and compare the areas of two-dimensional figures.
agenda:
Day 1 – Monday: Check Your Readiness
Show what you already know about area, rectangles, parallel and perpendicular lines, and geometric figures. Explain your reasoning whenever possible.

Day 2 – Tuesday: Reasoning to Find Area
Tiling the Plane: Compare geometric patterns and explain how shapes cover a region without gaps or overlaps.
Finding Area by Decomposing and Rearranging: Find area by composing smaller shapes, decomposing figures, and rearranging pieces into familiar shapes.

Day 3 – Wednesday: MAP Test English
Complete the MAP English assessment carefully and give your best effort.

Day 4 – Thursday: MAP Test Math
Complete the MAP Mathematics assessment carefully, use scratch paper, and show perseverance.

Day 5 – Friday: Reasoning to Find Area
Use different strategies to find the area of polygons, compare strategies, explain your reasoning, and label answers with square units.
homework: Complete any assigned DeltaMath practice. Bring your notebook, paper, and a sharpened pencil to class every day.
languageObjectives: Students will explain that area is the amount of the plane covered by a two-dimensional region.
Students will compare and explain area strategies using the terms tile, compose, decompose, rearrange, and square units.

objectives: By the end of the week, students will build our classroom community, learn the routines and materials needed for math class, set up DeltaMath, and demonstrate what they remember from Grade 5 math.
agenda: Tuesday: Welcome to 6th Grade Math; make name tents; meet our class; review daily materials; receive an available take-home IM book; and begin the Grade 5 math diagnostic.
Wednesday: Complete the Grade 5 math diagnostic and register for DeltaMath.
Thursday: Practice our classroom routines and begin our first math lesson.
Friday: Continue the math lesson, share strategies, and reflect on our first week.
Name-Tent Directions: Fold an 8.5 × 11-inch sheet into thirds so it stands. Write your name large, dark, and easy to read. At the bottom, add one sport or activity you enjoy.
Daily Materials: Bring a notebook, paper, and a pencil to every class.
homework: Bring your notebook, paper, and a pencil every day. Keep your assigned math book at home for review.
languageObjectives: Students will introduce themselves and share one sport or activity they enjoy.
Students will explain their mathematical thinking and describe the strategies they use.
